World Bank unhappy over fund diversion from Balochistan. ISLAMABAD: Expressing serious displeasure over reputational challenges, the World Bank has warned that redirecting funds from a multi-billion-rupee resilient housing programme for the flood-affected population to infrastructure projects would further aggravate poverty in Balochistan. “Based on the socio-economic profile of the eligible household, the risk is not simply that households remain without housing assistance; rather, it is that existing vulnerabilities become mutually reinforcing and deepen over time,” the World Bank said in detailed communication to the federal and Balochistan governments. In this case, 84 per cent of eligible beneficiaries are ultra-poor and vulnerable, with 28pc earning less than $30 and another 26pc earning between $31 and $70 per month, while 39pc are tenants, 37pc are daily-wage labourers and 8pc are small farmers. These groups typically have limited savings, weak access to formal credit, few productive assets and low capacity to absorb shocks, WB said. After meetings with the federal minister for planning, the chief minister of Balochistan and others following the capping of housing support at 62,966 first-tranche beneficiaries as of June 22, 2026, and subsidy support to 97,000, World Bank’s country director Boloromaa Amgaabazar expressed concern over the decision as well as the handling of issues pertaining to fraud and corruption. Cautions exclusion could deepen poverty, disaster risks, social tensions She wrote to the federal secretaries for economic affairs and planning, as well as the secretary of Balochistan, that the capping and redirection of housing support was leaving 119,049 verified and eligible households without identified financing support. Its public disclosure before the finalisation of a jointly agreed communication strategy with the bank had also created risks, as households that had completed verification and signed the project undertakings might continue to expect housing assistance. She wrote that 66,120 exclusion-related grievances had been registered in the project grievance management system on or before the agreed cut-off date. Therefore, each complainant should be contacted individually and formally notified of the decision. “Written acknowledgment, or other verifiable evidence confirming delivery and receipt of the communication, should be obtained and shared with the bank for review. A credible and transparent grievance resolution process is essential to mitigating legal, operational, and reputational risks associated with eventual closure of the component,” Ms Amgaabazar wrote. With the capping of housing support, eligible but excluded households may face a compounding cycle of vulnerability that not only reinforces poverty but increases it, raises disaster risk and undermines long-term recovery and resilience, diminishing the objectives with which the project was initiated. With limited resources, families may be forced to divert income from essential needs such as food, healthcare and education towards continued temporary shelter repairs, while also resorting to debt or the sale of productive assets to cope. At the same time, families unable to rebuild resilient homes may remain in damaged or unsafe structures, leaving them more exposed to recurring floods, storms, earthquakes and heatwaves. On top of that, the exclusion of verified eligible beneficiaries may also generate grievances, perceptions of inequity and unfairness, and continued erosion of trust in government institutions and development programmes, risks that have been observed in other housing reconstruction operations. Meta launches AI model as Zuckerberg champions open-weight push. Menlo Park (California): Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg called for lower US barriers for open-source AI to better compete with Chinese rivals as the social media giant released a new open-weight model on Monday and said more would follow soon. The new model, Muse Glimmer, is smaller than leading AI models from rivals and is instead designed to run agentic tasks on a Mac or PC with a single graphics card, aiming to tap demand for AI systems that run directly on people’s devices. “We’ve got even bigger models that are coming soon,” Zuckerberg said in a video post accompanying his 14-page essay titled The Future is for Everyone in which he championed spreading AI rather than leaving it in the hands of a few. “The notion AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic.” Zuckerberg’s statement marks the latest show of support for open-weight AI, which is gaining traction as businesses grow wary of ballooning AI bills and worry about recent cybersecurity incidents involving models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. Open-weight models are typically cheaper than leading models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. Th­­­­ey also come with publicly accessible core components for easy customisation, unlike closed models that companies keep fully under their control. Those controls are in the spotlight after Hugging Face, the AI coding collaboration hacked by a rogue OpenAI model, was forced to use a Chinese open-weight model to defend against the attack because closed-source models have curbs on cybersecurity use. Chinese startups are leading the race for open-weight models, with Moonshot’s Kimi K3, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Max and DeepSeek’s V4-Flash rivaling the performance of top US systems. By contrast, the leading models from US developers OpenAI, Anthropic and Alphabet’s Google are closed-weight. Shares of Meta, which have fallen about 10pc so far this year, were up nearly 3pc in premarket trading on Monday. Policy rethink Meta also plans to release the weights of Muse Spark 1.2, its most advanced model, built by a costly superintelligence team it formed last year to claw its way back into the AI race. The company had long supported open models and was among the only US tech firms to release such models before poor reception for its Llama 4 last year forced a change in strategy. In Monday’s wide-ranging AI essay, Zuckerberg also unveiled a new $1 billion fund that aims to ease fears about the impact of its data-center build-out by offering support to communities. Growing local opposition to data centres has become a key election iss­ue in the US and one of the biggest hur­­dles for Big Tech’s push to build the infrastructure needed to power AI. “One significant disadvantage that the U.S. has compared to countries like China is that it is more difficult to build infrastructure here,” Zuckerberg, whose company is set to spend as much as $145 billion this year on AI infrastructure, said. Zuckerberg also said the US needed to rethink policies if domestic firms were to lead in open-weight models, including on data use and distillation — a method that uses the outputs of a powerful AI system to train a smaller model that can handle some of the same tasks with far less computing power. He said that Meta would implement a governance structure to give its independent directors the power to approve the safety criteria for rele­asing models. “Foreign labs curren­tly hold several advantages here sin­ce American labs have to comply wi­­­­­th many additional restrictions on training data,” Zuckerberg said. Topic of no importance. THE past couple of weeks have been packed with news and not just of the international kind. There were elections in Azad Kashmir , verbal duelling between the PPP and PML-N and an intense debate on a system that has collapsed. And in the midst of this came the matter of superior sounding administrative units versus local governments. What more could a journalist want? Yet more bad news it seems. For there was a relatively unimportant news item in the oft-ignored city pages of this paper, which announced a new underpass at the injunction of Margalla Road and Eighth Avenue. It seems as if someone, somewhere in the hallways of CDA has decided the short wait at the crossing is a wait too long. And Dubai-like, the rich residents of Islamabad should also not have to wait at all, for modernity means zooming around wide roads. So a new underpass the city shall have — at a junction where the avenue is called Faisal Avenue, for it leads up to the mosque, in the green lap of the Margallas. It is hard to keep count of the underpasses and flyovers CDA has inflicted upon this small city, especially in recent times. The new boss of the city, Mohsin Naqvi, is surely inspired by his boss, Shehbaz Sharif. As chief minister of Punjab, Naqvi was praised for his ‘Mohsin speed’, a term which paid homage to him and Shehbaz Sharif who too had been awarded a similar epithet. Both were praised for the speed at which they built projects. It’s hard to keep count of the underpasses and flyovers CDA has inflicted on Islamabad. In a country where visible brick-and-mortar projects pass for development, speed is seen as a virtue, rather than decision-making which is sustainable and helps improve people’s lot. And while Shehbaz junior now does illustrate the difference between building bridges and running a country, Naqvi has brought the speedy flair to Islamabad, where CDA has built flyovers in every nook and cranny of the city that can fit one. After all, if Shehbaz Sharif could take away university land to build roads, why can’t others build on existing roads? In so doing, the current government has contributed to turning a small green city into a grey shadow of Lahore. It is more unfortunate for the capital, for Islamabad has little of the old charm or history that Lahore can lay claim to. The greenery and hills are all the capital can offer but between its rapid expansion, numerous housing societies, and our planners’ obsession with Dubai-style traffic, Islamabad is losing its uniqueness. Over time, the construction is also becoming as durable as the governments in Islamabad. Each time, it rains, a newly built road reveals the poor standards of construction, so much so that media organisations are stopped from covering the quick wear and tear. This was seen when the roads in front of a known hotel needed quick repairs after rain, and when a fancy sculpture at a new roundabout couldn’t withstand a monsoon spell. But it was perhaps just a coincidence for had the construction standards been really poor, more attention would have been paid to another news story that got very little attention. Recently, a story appeared in a paper about audit objections to the new underpass built near the F-9 park in Islamabad. It reported that the audit highlighted faults in the design of the underpass. However, the little attention that was paid to the story shows it really wasn’t all that significant or newsworthy. My objections however are different. Dangerous turns in underpasses, which require cars to suddenly slow down, are hardly important in a city built for speed — half of Islamabad is now built to allow vehicles to zip around. However, why do those running this city want ugly bridges and underpasses near the F-9 park? For those who are unfamiliar with Islamabad, the F-9 park comprises an entire sector in the heart of the city and perhaps is comparable to Central Park in Manhattan, New York. Anywhere else in the world, such a large green space would be protected and so would the real estate around it. But not in Islamabad. Years ago, a part of it was given to an international franchise; despite a court order, the city found a way to let the corner be, and even give it legal cover. Now, two sides of the park boast flyovers that obstruct the view of the greenery. Imagine if someone suggested constructing bridges on Fifth Avenue next to Central Park. In Pakistan, we have no such concerns. Cars have a need to speed through signal-free corridors — and if it means ruining the roads and the serene views next to the city’s green spaces, so be it. And now Faisal Avenue is next. It is a wide road so named because it leads down to the Faisal Mosque, synonymous with Islamabad in some ways. The decision, it seems, has been made — and with little input from either the city’s residents or others. If some feel the idea is not a good one, there is little that can be done about it. And neither can the courts provide a recourse — for obvious reasons. It may seem like a frivolous issue to write about at a time when so much is happening in the country and the region, but there is a point to be made here. The local government or smaller provincial debate is not an abstract one about what theory says. And neither will it yield the results its proponents are boasting about if the representatives are not accountable to the people. And accountability, first and foremost, comes from genuine representation. If the residents of Islamabad had that, instead of bureaucrats and MNAs with controversial electoral wins, perhaps some of this construction could have been questioned. The writer is a journalist. Equal citizens. AUG 11 occupies a special place in our history because it was on this day in 1947 that Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah set out what citizenship in the new state ought to mean. Addressing the Constituent Assembly, he spoke of a country in which people were free to go to their temples, mosques or other places of worship, and where religion, caste or creed would not determine their standing before the state. He insisted that citizens should enjoy equal rights, privileges and obligations, and that discrimination between communities had no place in the order Pakistan was attempting to build. These remarks formed part of a wider vision of government based on law, impartiality, protection of life and property, and the safeguarding of religious belief. It is fitting, then, that minority rights activists will gather outside Mazar-i-Quaid in Karachi today to recall that promise and demand that it be honoured. The Minority Rights March has put forward 11 demands, including stronger safeguards against forced conversions, protection from the misuse of blasphemy laws, greater political representation, removal of discriminatory material from textbooks, protection of minority properties and places of worship, and expanded access to education and employment. Organisers have also called for constitutional amendments allowing non-Muslim citizens to qualify for the offices of president and prime minister. Whether every demand commands consensus is a matter for democratic debate. But the principle from which they proceed — that citizenship should not be graded according to faith — should not be controversial in a republic that continues to invoke Jinnah as its founding authority. The delay in a written NOC for the march deserves attention. Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favour. The gap between Jinnah’s principle of equal citizenship and present realities cannot be ignored. It is especially troubling because these protections were articulated at the birth of Pakistan itself. Religious minorities continue to face mob violence, attacks on their places of worship, forced conversions and social and economic exclusion. Laws intended to protect religion have at times been weaponised through false accusations, with consequences extending far beyond the courtroom. Even where the state guarantees equality, social prejudice and institutional barriers make that guarantee fragile in practice. National Minority Rights Day must be more than a ceremonial observance. It should prompt the state to examine where law, policy and public culture continue to fall short of the standard articulated on Aug 11, 1947. Jinnah did not ask minorities to be grateful for protection; he described equal citizenship as a fundamental principle. Pakistan cannot honour that principle through speeches alone. It will honour it when every citizen, regardless of faith, can claim the same dignity, security and political belonging. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

The tipping point of change. DISCUSSIONS are happening about how so many of the young protesters that rocked the Modi government recently came from families that have been faithfully voting for the right-wing prime minister. A crucial fact that seems to elude the discussants is that liberal or communist or fascist ideologues are not hatched in hatcheries. Unlike Narendra Modi, they are not ‘non-biological’ beings that gatecrash our earthly world. To begin with, it would be useful to bear in mind that the jailed left-wing student leader Umar Khalid had transcended to secular left politics from circumstances in which his father was a member of a major Muslim revivalist body. Likewise, Neha Bora, president of the pro-communist All-India Students’ Association who fasted for 23 days at the protest, tells you sans demur that she broke away from a family tradition of voting for the Muslim-baiting BJP. The flow can be in the opposite direction too. Howard Fast, as the despairing chief of the US Communist Party, famed for writing the story of Spartacus, the slave rebel of Rome, became a Buddhist seeker after abandoning Marxism. Numerous such examples abound in the Indian intellectual pantheon of progressivism and regression, which we can discuss. A scene is vivid from my childhood in which the migration to progressive politics would seem facile despite the good intentions. It was a balmy morning in Mustafabad, a village of erstwhile Shia taluqdars in the heart of Uttar Pradesh. Some young men and women in the joint family had recently got the first university degrees. Marxism was in the air in university campuses in the 1960s. That morning the tea was of just the right temperature, its bouquet flavourful. Three bespectacled young men from among the learned ones were steeped in a discussion that straddled Marx, Nehru, Josh and Neruda. The men were wrapped in embroidered woollen shawls over spotless white muslin kurta-pajama attires when the mehtrani, the woman carrying human refuse in an open reed basket, walked past. Other than putting the handkerchiefs on their faces briefly, the men remained unabashedly unperturbed in their intellectual chatter. A follower of Dalit politics would have reacted differently to the brutal absurdness of the frame. Indian communists added B.R. Ambedkar and the sickening caste angle to their class analysis grudgingly, only recently harnessing it to the dialectical quiver. These early activists had the theory but not the praxis, which would take years to arrive, or perhaps not. It’s not clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. Thus, it’s not even clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day to scare the hell out of a stubborn authoritarian government had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. A Buddhist would call the migration nirvana — the blowing out of greed, hatred and ignorance. Collectively, the youth displayed a healthy mix of all three characteristics. When and if they reassemble it could be a different variety of mix. Arvind Kejriwal had held out a similar promise when his Aam Aadmi Party stop­ped the Hindutva juggernaut in Delhi in 2015. The ‘Modi wave’ had taken care of Maharashtra and Haryana state polls in quick succession. Kejriwal stopped the BJP chariot in Delhi. Then something equally important occurred. He rejected the offer of support from the Shahi Imam of Jama Masjid, and people were emboldened to believe that the time had come to separate religion from politics as the constitution ordains. Then in a crude display of regressive religiosity, he started holding election campaigns from Hindu temples and wooed senior voters with offers of free Hindu pilgrimages. One doesn’t have to agree with T.S. Eliot who says: “Youth is cruel and has no remorse. And smiles at situations it cannot see.” But youth is a handy demographic factor with an uncertain political trajectory. Not long ago, taking on the same Modi establishment, a courageous woman had single-handedly instigated the downfall of Modi’s minister accused of sexual transgressions. But the same charges failed to secure the conviction of a BJP muscleman. However, there again is the unforgettable instance of determined and seasoned farmers who forced the cancellation of Modi’s prized anti-farm laws. It is heartening to remember, therefore, that the Cockroach leaders have committed themselves to deter violations of citizen’s voting rights by a wayward election commission. The youth are committed to take on the hopelessly compromised corporate media that misreported the protests. Keeping company in the progressive transition of Khalid and Bora are some very eminent intellectuals of the subcontinent. Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s path from traditional Islamic education to becoming one of South Asia’s most iconic Marxist intellectuals highlights a fascinating evolution. Majro­­oh Sultanpuri was destined to become a hakim, for which he had acquired a degree. Then he turned towards left politics and endured isolation and even jail for his beliefs. I recently saw lovely pictures of Faiz’s daughters on a holiday in Sri Lanka. Had DPT been around, they would have in all likelihood been in India for he had the magic of fixing visas for all manner of progressive Pakis­tanis. Devi Prasad Tripathi came to JNU from the RSS stable. He became a staunch member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist and won the election as student union president when he was arrested and jailed during the emergency. Many political stalwarts left the RSS to become leftists and are leading critics of the Modi establishment. Kaifi Azmi became a progressive writer after early inspiration from the valour of Imam Husain. And, Iran has shown that a just battle can harness religious motifs to thwart a powerful aggressor. “ Dekhna Kaifi nishan-i-hurriyat lahraega/ Jab jahan ko azm-i-Sher-i-Karbala mil jayaega ” (‘Watch, O Kaifi, the banner of freedom shall flutter high/ Once the world finds the Lion of Karbala and joins his battle cry’). Kaifi’s pre-Marxist verses presaged the retreat of imperialism not far from the site of the students’ protest. And Iran’s left? They’re cohabiting with imperialism. President Zardari approves additional judges' appointments to high courts, ending weeks-long deadlock. ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday gave his assent to the appointment of additional judges for the five high courts, along with confirmation of some as permanent judges, ending a weeks-long deadlock between the Presidency and the government over the judicial appointments. “The president has approved the appointment of additional judges in the Lahore High Court (LHC), Sindh High Court (SHC), Peshawar High Court (PHC), Islamabad High Court (IHC), and Balochistan High Court (BHC),” the Presidency said in a statement. It added that he had also given his assent to the confirmation of certain additional judges of SHC and LHC as permanent judges. The president gave his assent to the summary forwarded by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, which was based on the recommendations of the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP), official sources confirmed on Tuesday. The appointments and confirmations were pending since July 20 and 21, when the JCP — the body responsible for appointing judges to the superior judiciary — recommended them. The JCP had recommended the confirmation of four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court, a six-month extension for an additional judge of the SHC, and the appointment of 19 additional judges to the Lahore, Islamabad, Sindh and Balochistan high courts. Under Clause 8 of Article 175-A of the Cons­titution, the recommendations were forwarded to the prime minister, who then sent the summary to the president. However, the summary had remained pending with the president since then. The president’s legal team had raised certain objections to the JCP proceedings, noting that nearly all nominees proposed by the PPP were rejected. They had also conveyed that some candidates recommended for appointment had criminal records. Meanwhile, the delay in the presidential assent had begun to affect the functioning of the superior judiciary and created practical complications. Four additional judges of the PHC, whose confirmations were recommended by the JCP, ceased to hold office after their tenure expired on August 4 due to the absence of formal notifications. Similarly, an additional judge of the SHC, whose term had already been extended by six months once, relinquished office after his tenure expired on July 29. Amid the stalemate, the government had also been examining the possibility of invoking Article 48(1) of the Constitution to issue the notifications through the law ministry, arguing that the president was required to act on the summary within a fortnight of its submission — a period that has since expired. However, government functionaries later maintained that with the matter now sub judice, notifications could not be issued at this stage. Sources had said the government’s legal team planned to pursue an “out-of-court” settlement with its counterparts at the Presidency. For its part, the Presidency’s legal team had contended that Article 175-A did not prescribe a specific timeframe for the president’s action and that the provision could not be overridden by Article 48(1) to bypass the Presidency. They had also referred to Article 48(2), which empowered the president “to act in his discretion in respect of any matter in respect of which he is empowered by the Constitution to do so” and states that the validity of anything done by the president shall not be called into question on any ground whatsoever. On the other hand, government sources had maintained that judicial appointments were governed by constitutional provisions and that any deadlock must be resolved strictly in accordance with the Constitution. Meanwhile, a plea challenging the delay in the president’s approval had also been filed in the IHC. The IHC reserved its verdict on the maintainability of a petition filed by advocate Luqman Chaudhary through his counsel Zahid Chaudhry on Monday, seeking a direction to the president to approve the summary. Other approvals Apart from giving his nod to the judges’ appointments and confirmations, President Zardari also approved the equalisation of the salaries, allowances, and pensions of Supreme Court judges with those of judges of the Federal Constitutional Court. Moreover, he approved amendments to the 1997 order relating to the leave, pensions, and privileges of high court judges, the Presidency said, adding that he also gave his assent to the appointment of Haroon Akhtar as advisor to the prime minister on industries and production.
